ls.lead: One idea, one gesture, one question. Each right answer stamps your passport.

items.alt: Kūro, sitting on a suitcase, catches an envelope carried by a paper plane
items.d: A client abroad can pay you by four routes. None is the best everywhere: compare the delay, the fees and what your bank accepts.

pick.v: The client wires money to your account. They need your IBAN or account number, your bank’s SWIFT/BIC code and an invoice. Ask your bank first how it receives a transfer from abroad, and in which currency it is credited.

An online service collects the money for you and pays it out to your account or card. Check first, on the service’s own site, that it opens accounts for residents of your country and how money is withdrawn.

The platform charges the client, holds the money until delivery, takes its commission and pays you the rest. Simple to start with: read its commission and its withdrawal methods before you accept a job.
The client sends tokens, often a stablecoin, to your address. It is fast and cannot be undone. Legal in some countries, banned in others, Algeria among them (law 25-10): check the law where you live.

items.q: Before you accept a first payment from abroad, what do you check first?
a: How your bank or the service receives the money, and what it costs you
items.ok: Yes. The route first, the price after.

items.alt: Kūro peeks out of a small vault door, in front of a card and three coins
items.d: A multi-currency account holds several currencies side by side and gives you bank details to be paid with. What costs is almost never the opening: it is three fees.

pick.v: The margin taken when one currency becomes another. Compare the rate you are offered with the market rate on the same day: the gap is your real price.
A fixed amount or a percentage on each sending, each receipt or each withdrawal. A small percentage weighs a lot on a large invoice.
Fees at the cash machine, abroad, or beyond a monthly limit. Read the fee table before you travel, not after.

items.listT: Four questions to ask before you open one
list: Does the service accept residents of my country?
In which currencies can I receive?
How do I withdraw, and at what price?
Who holds and protects my money?
items.q: Two services both say “0 fees”. Where do you look?
items.ok: Yes. A rate worse than the market is a fee that does not say its name.

items.alt: Kūro rests a paw on an abacus, beside a calendar and an hourglass
items.d: A rate is not guessed, it is worked out: what you want to keep, plus your costs, divided by the days you really bill.

f.fine: Your reliable income covers your spending: the savings do not move.

src.title: The course’s sources
src.note: Every figure in this course comes from one of these sources. Where a study is small, or a figure is the company’s own, the level says so.

items.d: Gamification borrows a few of a game’s springs for an activity that is not a game: a course, an app, a site. The activity stays the real thing; the game lends it its way of making you want to.

pick.v: “The use of game design elements in non-game contexts”: the definition proposed by Deterding and colleagues in 2011, the one research has used since.
It is not building a whole game, and it is not a coat of paint. If you take the game away and nothing useful is left, it was not gamification.
In 2010 the game designer Margaret Robertson wrote that the right word for what she was seeing was “pointsification”: points and badges put on anything, without the game.

items.q: Which of the three is gamification?
a: A progress bar in an online course
items.ok: Yes. The course is still a course; the bar lends it one of a game’s springs: seeing that you are moving forward.

items.d: A good game does not hold you with its points. It feeds three needs psychology has long described: to feel capable, to feel free, to feel connected. When an activity feeds them, people come back without being pushed.

pick.v: Immediate feedback and steps within reach: you can see yourself improve. That is the need for competence.
You choose your path and your pace. What becomes compulsory stops being a game. That is the need for autonomy.
Playing with others, or belonging to a shared world. That is the need for relatedness.
From Ryan and Deci’s self-determination theory (2000): three psychological needs, competence, autonomy and relatedness. Satisfied, they strengthen motivation; thwarted, they weaken it.

items.q: A progress bar feeds which need first?
items.ok: Yes: it shows the road already covered. It is competence made visible.

items.d: Does it really help people learn? In 2020 Sailer and Homner pooled 38 publications, 40 experiments in all. Their answer: yes, effects that are small but real, and not all equally solid.

pick.v: On what is learned: g = 0.49. It is the study’s most stable result, even when only the most rigorous experiments are kept.
On motivation: g = 0.36. The authors call it less stable than the first.
On what people actually do: g = 0.25, the smallest of the three, and also less stable.

Two wider reviews say it another way. Hamari and colleagues (2014, 24 studies): positive effects that depend greatly on the context and on the people. Koivisto and Hamari (2019, 819 studies): results that lean positive, with a remarkable share of mixed results.

items.q: What should you take from these studies?
a: It helps a little, when it is well designed for its audience
items.ok: Yes: real, modest effects that depend on the context. Nobody serious promises more.

items.d: A game mechanic answers one precise spring. You choose one or two for a goal, not ten for decoration.

pick.v: Nunes and Drèze (2006): a task of eight steps presented as ten steps with two already done is completed more often, and faster. Starting at 2 of 10 commits you more than starting at 0 of 8.
Kivetz and colleagues (2006), in a real café: the closer customers get to the free coffee, the more often they buy. People speed up near the finish line.
On Stack Overflow, Anderson and colleagues (2013) see activity rise as a badge nears, then fall back. A 2020 study adds a caveat: about 20% of users respond.

Duolingo told its shareholders in November 2026 that it runs hundreds of experiments, on notifications and streaks among other things, to bring users back: 64.9 million a day in the third quarter of 2026.
Completing a set of things: that is what this course’s eight stickers do. The mechanic is in front of you.

items.q: Two loyalty cards both ask for eight car washes. Which one is completed more often?
items.ok: Yes. The same effort, but you have already started: that is the endowed progress effect.

items.t: What it does for a brand
items.d: This level is our reading as practitioners, not a study’s result. A game gives a brand three things a logo alone does not: a voice, a world, and a reason to come back.

pick.v: Here, Kūro judges your answers in two words. A brand that reacts to what you do has a character; a brand that recites has none.
The night workshop, the radio, the DOURO·8 console, the seals: it all comes from the same place. You recognise the brand without seeing its logo.
Stamps, seals, stickers: small ends to reach, which give a reason to finish the page and to come back to it.
If the game hides the offer, the price or the contact, it works against the brand. The game serves the message; it does not replace it.

items.q: What does a brand gain first from being playable?
a: A character people recognise and come back to
items.ok: Yes. The rest may follow, but character is what brings people back.

items.d: Four cases, each with its source and its limit. Two figures come from the companies themselves, and a third from a brand campaign: each time, it is said.

pick.v: The Starbucks Rewards programme has 35.8 million active members in the United States, and 59% of the money taken in the chain’s own U.S. stores comes from its members. Figures published by Starbucks for the quarter ended in late June 2026.
Deloitte added game elements to its executive training platform. Harvard Business Review (2013) reports 37% more users returning to it each week. A company figure, with no comparison group.

An online game in which players fold proteins. In 2011 its players produced, in three weeks, a model accurate enough for researchers to determine the structure of an enzyme from a monkey retrovirus. The result was published in Nature Structural & Molecular Biology.

Stockholm, 2010: for three days, drivers who kept to the limit were entered in a lottery. The average speed reported fell from 32 to 25 km/h. A famous case but a fragile one: three days, no control group, and a figure given by the sponsor, Volkswagen.

items.q: Which of these cases rests on a scientific publication?
items.ok: Yes. The others are company or campaign figures: useful, and to be read as such.

items.d: A game can also demotivate, push and trap. Knowing where it breaks is part of the craft.

pick.v: Lepper, Greene and Nisbett (1973): children who already liked an activity showed less interest in it after doing it for a promised reward. Those who got a surprise reward, or none, kept their interest.

Hanus and Fox (2015) followed two classes for sixteen weeks. The one with badges and a leaderboard ended less motivated, less satisfied, and with lower exam scores. A small study, but a warning: a leaderboard is not a gift to everyone.

In November 2012 the analyst firm Gartner forecast that 80% of the gamified applications of the time would miss their business objectives by 2014, mainly because of poor design. It is a forecast, not a measurement.

In 2022 the U.S. consumer protection agency (FTC) published a report on “dark patterns”, interfaces that push people into choices they would not otherwise have made. The same year the maker of Fortnite agreed to pay 245 million dollars to refund unwanted purchases.

items.q: According to Gartner, why were most of these projects going to fail?
a: People do not like to play
items.ok: Yes. It is not the game that fails, it is the game badly thought out for its goal.

items.d: This site plays, and it has given itself rules. Here they are, with the place to check them.

pick.v: The radio, the clips, Kūro: everything waits for your move, and everything stops with one. On a device set to “reduce motion”, nothing moves.
The DOURO·8 calculator looks like a console, but its receipt adds up lines and its total is their exact sum. The game makes the price readable; it does not dress it up.
Seven seals open a drawing. Eight levels give eight stickers. No reward here is traded for your address or for a purchase.
Stamps, seals and stickers stay in your browser. They are sent nowhere; there is no account and no leaderboard.
No streak to keep, no countdown. You can leave and come back: your progress waits for you.

items.q: On this site, what do you get for seven seals?
items.ok: Yes. That is our rule: we reward with something to look at, never with pressure to buy.

src.title: The road book’s sources
src.note: The advice on security, backups, bandwidth and stays comes from these sources; the calculators’ figures are your own. The ANSSI guide dates from 2019 and addresses employees: its habits hold for a freelancer too. Nothing here is legal or tax advice.

items.d: Clients do not fall from the sky: they answer messages. How many should you send? It can be counted. The clients you want, divided by the share of people who reply, then by the share of those who sign.

f.unit: The starting rates are examples, not averages. Note what you send and what comes back for a month, then put in your own.

items.q: You send 40 messages: 4 people reply, 1 signs. You want 3 clients a month. What do you do?
a: Send 120 messages, or improve one of the two rates
Wait for word of mouth to do the rest
items.ok: Yes. One signature per 40 messages, so 120 messages for 3 clients. Or a better message, or a better offer: both rates can be worked on.

items.d: A project price is time counted before you start: your day rate, times the days you estimate, plus a margin for what you did not see coming. The client wants one figure that no longer moves.

f.dep: at the order, if you ask for 40%
f.unit: In whatever currency you type. To find your day rate:

items.q: The project takes three days more than planned, and the scope has not changed. Who pays for those three days?
a: The client: you send an extra invoice
You: that is what the margin is for
items.ok: Yes, if the price was firm. It is the Studio’s rule: “if the work overruns, the difference is on us”. If the scope changes, that is a new quote.

items.d: A signed quote prevents most disputes, because it answers the awkward questions in advance. Here are five lines, with what the Studio writes in its own. These are our terms, not a legal template.

pick.v: What is included, written as a list: the pages, the languages, the functions. What is not on it is not included. Every other line depends on this one.
At the Studio: 40% at the order, on a signed quote, and 60% at delivery, before the site goes live. A deposit shows the project is real on both sides.
At the Studio: two rounds of revisions per stage, design then development, are included; further ones are quoted separately. Without this line, a project never ends.
At the Studio: once the site is paid in full, it belongs to the client, with the code, the design files and the content. Write down the moment the work changes hands.
At the Studio: the firm deadline is set once the project has been scoped together, not before. A deadline promised before the scope is known is a guess.

items.q: The client asks for a third round of revisions on the design. What does the Studio’s quote say?
items.ok: Yes. Two rounds per stage are included; further ones are quoted separately.

items.d: A client six time zones away is not a problem, it is a calendar. What matters is the hours your two working days share: that is where calls go. The rest is done in writing.

f.none: No shared hour between two 9-to-18 days: one of you will have to shift theirs, or everything goes in writing.
f.unit: Two 9-to-18 days, in whole hours. Algeria is on UTC+1 all year, with no summer time; the client’s summer time, if they have one, can move the window by an hour.

items.q: You are on UTC+1, your client on UTC−5. At what time, on your clock, do you offer the call?
items.ok: Yes. 16:00 for you is 10:00 for your client: the hour falls inside both days.

items.d: Your office fits in a bag: anything that breaks, gets lost or cuts out stops you dead. Three precautions: copies of your files, enough bandwidth for your calls, and a second connection.

pick.v: At least three copies of your files, on two devices, with one backup kept somewhere else. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls it a popular strategy that can be used in most scenarios: if one copy is compromised, at least one other is intact.

A one-to-one call needs little. Zoom recommends 600 kbps each way for high-quality video, and 1.2 Mbps for 720p; on a group call, 1 Mbps up and 600 kbps down, and at 720p 2.6 Mbps up and 1.8 Mbps down. Google Meet counts up to 1.7 Mbps per participant at 720p, and lowers the definition when bandwidth is short. These are the vendors’ own figures: test your connection before the call, not during it.
The Wi-Fi where you stay can drop on the day of a call. Keep a second way in: your phone’s hotspot. It is also what the NCSC advises instead of an unknown hotspot: use the mobile network.

items.q: Your bag is stolen: the laptop, and the backup drive that was inside it. What was missing?
items.ok: Yes. That is the “1” in 3-2-1: one copy outside the bag, online or with someone you trust.

items.d: On the road, your accounts are worth more than your gear: a laptop can be bought again, a hacked mailbox much less so. Five habits, each recommended by a public cyber security agency.

pick.v: The French agency, ANSSI, advises avoiding networks you do not control whenever possible: hotel, station or café Wi-Fi. The UK’s NCSC agrees: the simplest precaution is not to connect through an unknown hotspot and to use the mobile network instead; a VPN is another option.
The NCSC recommends turning on 2-step verification for your most important accounts: email, banking, social media, online shopping. It keeps criminals out even if they know your password.
A different password for each account, says ANSSI. And a password manager to remember them for you, says the NCSC, which also advises choosing passkeys wherever they are offered.

The NCSC advises that every laptop use encryption that requires a password to boot: BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS. Keep the recovery key somewhere safe. And before you leave, ANSSI advises finding out about the law of the country you are going to, including on encryption.

Three habits from ANSSI’s guide for professionals who travel: lock your session whenever you step away, even for a moment; do not plug in a USB key you were given without having it checked; carry the strict minimum of data.

items.q: At the airport, you need to sign in to an important account. What is safest?
items.ok: Yes. The mobile network rather than a network you do not control: that is the NCSC’s advice, and ANSSI’s.

items.d: A year has 52 weeks, but you bill only part of it: there are holidays, public holidays, illness, and all the work nobody pays for. Count your billed days before you promise yourself an income.

f.unit: Holidays, public holidays and illness go into the weeks without work. The starting billed share is an example: measure your own.

items.q: You work 5 days a week and bill 60% of them. Over one week, that makes…
items.ok: Yes. The other two days are real: prospecting, quotes, paperwork, learning. Your day rate is what pays for them.

items.d: Going to work somewhere else means four files to open before you buy the ticket: the stay, taxes, health, the bank. The answers depend on your nationality, your status and the country. This lesson gives you the questions, not the answers.

pick.v: Every country has its own rules on entry and length of stay. One official example: in the Schengen area, a short stay is usually a maximum of 90 days within any 180-day period, and the European Commission publishes a calculator to check it. To ask the consulate: does this visa allow me to work remotely for clients in another country?

Where do you pay tax if you spend several months elsewhere? It depends on your tax residence, and on the agreements between the two countries. To ask the tax office or an accountant, before leaving: from when am I a resident here, and what must I still declare at home?
To ask your insurer: am I covered outside my country, for how long, and for repatriation? And the consulate: does my visa require insurance?
To check before you go: does my card work abroad, and at what cost? Does my bank send its codes by text message, and will my number receive them there? Who receives my post in the meantime?

items.q: You leave the Schengen area for one day, then come back. The 90-day count…
a: carries on: it looks at the previous 180 days
items.ok: Yes. You count back 180 days from each day of your stay: leaving for a day erases nothing. The Commission’s calculator does the count for you.

items.t: The logo is not the brand
items.d: A logo is delivered, and nothing changes: a logo is only a sign. Around it come the identity (colours, letters, pictures), the system (the rules that keep it consistent) and the brand: what people say about you when you are not in the room. For the Design Council, the UK’s design body, “your brand is more than a logo”: first sort what you have.

sort.aria: Sort four items into the four layers

rows.k: The drawn symbol and name
rows.why: The sign itself: that is the logo.

rows.k: The colour palette
rows.why: The visual language: people know you without the logo.

rows.k: The rule “never the logo on red”
rows.why: A rule that keeps everything consistent: the system.

items.q: A designer delivers a fine logo, alone, in one file. What do you have?
a: A sign: the identity and the rules are still to do
items.ok: Yes. A sign is the start. The rest is decided first.

keep.note: Not sure? Step 5 lets you see your own logo at 16 pixels.

no: No. The brand is what people say about you: a file does not hold that.
No. A system is written rules: a single file gives none.

items.d: “Everyone” is not an audience, and a logo made for everyone speaks to no one. The Design Council puts the target audience in every brief (the document that explains the project to the designer). Describe one person: what they want to get, where they find you, what makes them hesitate.

seek.ph: a cake ready at the time promised

doubt.ph: an order that once arrived late for a party

items.q: You like two logo routes (the designer’s first proposals) equally. How do you choose?
a: I take the one that speaks best to the person in my brief
I take the more colourful one
items.ok: Yes. Judge against the brief, not by taste: that is the Design Council’s advice.
no: Not quite. Your family is not your customer: judge against the brief, not by taste.
No. Colour is a means: the question is whom the route speaks to.

items.d: “The best quality”: your competitors say it too. A promise says what a client gets from you; a proof makes it believable: a written deadline, a figure to show, a signed review. Here a brief starts there: that is our method, not a rule.

promise.ph: made-to-order cakes ready at the agreed time

items.ex: For example: “made-to-order cakes ready at the agreed time, or refunded”; “a written quote that does not move, fitting included”. These are examples, not lines to copy.
items.proofPh: kneaded every morning, in view of the shop window

meter.none: For now, it is a slogan.
meter.weak: A promise. The proof is missing.

items.vague: “{w}” cannot be proved on its own: replace it with something a client can observe. For example: a deadline, a figure, a photo.
items.rule: The workshop’s rule: replace every adjective with a fact a client can observe.

grid.line: For {who}. What they want: {seek}. Our promise: {promise}. The proof: {proof}.
grid.note: The grid is our workshop’s: audience, need, promise, proof. The sentence under it goes into your brief.

items.q: Which promise can be proved?
a: “Delivered within 48 h, or delivery is free”
items.ok: Yes. A deadline can be checked. “Best” cannot.
no: No. “Best” cannot be observed: no customer can check it.
No. Passion cannot be shown: it takes a fact a customer can observe.

items.d: “I want blue”: and the designer has nothing left to look for. The Design Council advises describing the goal, not the solution. Say what people should feel, with three sliders: the designer chooses the means.

spec.t: The closest of our three identities
feel: AlmaFlowClim: clear, clean, cool. Two colours for cold and heat, a round and confident typeface.
tr4veler.exe: night, ink, one colour that shouts. Tight capitals, seals, a terminal’s tone.
Numidea Labs: paper, ink, a seal red. A heavy letter, a marker note.

voice.l: Three words people should say about you

items.q: What do you tell the designer?
a: “I want blue and a round typeface”
“We should come across as generous and careful, like a table laid for a celebration”
“Do what the competitor did, but better”
items.ok: Yes. The goal, not the means: they find the means.
no: No. That is already the solution: state the goal, the designer chooses the means.
No. Copying a competitor means being mistaken for them: say what people should feel with you.

l: A brand I like, and why (optional)
refs.ph: the name, then what you like: the colours, the tone, the packaging…
refs.note: Two are enough, if you say why: the “why” is what the designer uses.

items.d: Your printer asks for the logo for a 3-metre banner, and all you have is a JPEG. An identity is a set of files, and each one has a job. Open them one by one: they are the ones to look for in any proposal.

pick.v: A drawing made of shapes, not dots: for the printer, the sign, the banner. According to the web’s reference documentation (MDN), an SVG vector image renders at any size without loss of quality, unlike a PNG or a JPEG.
An image with no background, to place the logo on a document or a photo. It is a pixel image: we deliver it large enough for screens, and keep the vector for the rest.
Colour, one colour, black, white; long and square. For us, that is what stops the logo being squashed to fit somewhere.

The rule book: sizes, margins, colours, what is not allowed. It lets someone else make a consistent visual without calling you. Complete guidelines also give each colour a role (text, surface, accent, alert) and a reading order (title, details, action): that is our list. The W3C’s accessibility rules (WCAG 2.2) require a minimum contrast between text and its background: ask for a role per colour, and text that stays readable.
A font has a licence. The SIL OFL, a free licence for fonts, allows use in a logo and in print according to its own FAQ. For a paid font, ask who holds the licence and what it covers.

The guide by WIPO (the World Intellectual Property Organization) and INAPI for Algeria (2004) says it: the creator of a logo first holds its copyright; it advises settling this in the initial agreement, or having the right formally assigned to your company. In France, under the Intellectual Property Code, each right transferred must be named in the deed: ask for the assignment in writing.

pick.k: The campaign master and its formats
pick.v: One master file in separate layers (background, subject, text), then the formats cut from it, for example a square, a vertical story, a banner. With us, the master is kept and only what the frame shows changes; one page of rules says what may move and what may not.

items.q: For her second shop, the printer asks Nadia (our example) for the logo for a 3-metre banner. She sends…
a: a phone photo of the logo
the PNG from her social media page
items.ok: Yes. A vector stays sharp at any size; a pixel image does not.
no: No. A photo is made of dots: enlarged to 3 metres, it blurs.
No. A PNG is a pixel image, made for the screen: not for a banner.

items.d: “All included”, says the quote; and you do not know what “all” contains. The Design Council advises asking “Have you told me all the costs?” and “When does ownership of the design pass from the designer to us?”. rows.k: “Logo delivered as a JPEG, one file.”

rows.ask: The SVG/PDF files and every version of the logo

rows.k: “Three questions about your customers before drawing.”
rows.why: A good sign. The Design Council advises asking yourself whether the designer asked the right questions.

rows.k: “Price: all included.” No list.

rows.ours: With us: the base identity includes the logo (full, compact and one-ink), the colours, the type and the tone of voice. The “Full design kit” adds the guidelines, reusable components, the animated social media kit and the campaign master.
rows.ask: The written list of what is delivered

rows.k: Nothing about rights.
rows.why: Ask when the rights pass to you, and which ones, in writing.
rows.ours: With us: once the project is paid, you receive the vector sources and a written assignment of the rights that names the use, the place and the duration. We keep the right to show the work.
rows.ask: The assignment of rights in writing (use, place, duration)

rows.k: “Fonts under the OFL licence, usable for the logo.”
rows.why: Clear: the licence is named, and it covers a logo.
rows.ours: With us: fonts and photos follow the terms of their own licence.

rows.k: “A logo delivered in one day, with no questions about your customers.”
rows.why: Our workshop’s view: ask what is delivered and what the drawing is based on.
rows.ask: At least one conversation about my customers before drawing

rows.k: “Schedule: brief, routes, choice, finishing, delivery, each with a date.”
rows.why: A good sign: these are the stages the Design Council describes.
rows.ours: With us: two first routes, then three rounds of changes at each stage.

rows.k: “Colours: midnight blue and coral.” No roles, no contrast.
rows.why: Ask what each colour is for, and for text that stays readable on its background: the W3C’s accessibility rules (WCAG 2.2) set a minimum contrast.
rows.ask: A role for each colour, and text that stays readable

items.q: A proposal says “Price: all included”, with no list. You…
a: ask for the list of what is delivered
items.ok: Yes. Without a list, “all included” cannot be checked.
no: No. Without a list you do not know what “all” contains.
No. A discount on unknown contents still does not say what you receive.

items.t: The name, and whose it is
items.d: Your logo is drawn and paid for: it is not yet protected as a trademark. A mark is registered, country by country, with the national office, or through the Madrid System that WIPO runs. Pick a country to see whom to ask and what the official texts say.

pick.v: The office is INAPI; a mark lasts ten years, renewable. According to INPI’s sheet on Algeria (June 2025), INAPI itself examines whether the name is free, and a filer with no domicile in Algeria goes through an agent (someone who files in their name). The fees are on INAPI’s page: check them on the day you file.
pick.more: Also, according to the same sheet: registration takes about two years on average, a mark unused for more than three years is lost, and .dz names are reserved for entities established in Algeria or holders of a mark valid in Algeria.

pick.v: The office is INPI. A mark lasts ten years, renewable without limit, and must be used. INPI’s fee schedule applicable from 2 July 2026: filing €190 for one class (a category of goods or services), €40 per extra class, renewal €290 for one class. INPI’s search for earlier logos (marks already filed that look like yours) costs €532 for one class.

Registration is with the Ministry of Economy and Tourism. Its page lists AED 750 to apply, AED 750 for publication and AED 5,000 for registration, AED 6,500 in all, then 30 days for objections after publication. A foreign owner goes through an agent (someone who files in their name).

WIPO points to each national office, and to the Madrid System for several countries in one application. The question to ask the office: is this name free in my class (my category of goods or services)?

k: Reads and sounds right in Arabic, French and English

items.checkSrc: The list comes from the WIPO and INAPI guide: easy to read, say and remember, no unfortunate meaning in your languages, domain checked.

items.rights: And for an identity, once paid: the vector sources and a written assignment of the rights (use, place and duration named); we keep the right to show the work; fonts and photos follow their own licence.
items.q: Your logo is drawn and paid for. Is it protected as a trademark in Algeria?
a: No: it has to be filed with INAPI
Yes, if it is posted on your social media
items.ok: Yes. Filing is a separate step, country by country.

scripts.note: Each script has to be drawn: say so before the quote.

no: No. Filing is a separate step: nothing is automatic.
No. Posting is not filing: a mark is registered with the office.

You have a project: eight steps to tell the tool from the result, and leave with a brief that can be priced. pick.v: A ledger copied on many machines, where lines are added without rewriting the history. That is how NIST, the US standards agency, describes it.
An app or a device that keeps your keys. It does not hold the tokens: they stay on the network (ethereum.org, a community documentation site).
A line of the ledger that says who owns what: an interchangeable unit, or a unique object. What an NFT holder gets depends on what its creator set up (ethereum.org).

The site reads your public address; it can move nothing without your signature. But a signature can be a spending approval: according to ethereum.org it does not expire, disconnecting does not remove it, you have to revoke it. Connecting, signing a message and signing a transaction are three different requests: step 4 tells them apart.
The private key signs; the phrase recreates it. NIST puts it plainly: lose the key, lose the asset. The European authorities: never share it, whoever has it takes control.

A program published in the ledger. It runs as programmed when a transaction calls it, and its deployed code is public in the ledger. According to ethereum.org, once deployed it usually cannot be patched.
A token designed to track a currency. The European authorities warn it may not stay so stable, especially when markets are under stress.
Every action pays the network, and the amount moves with demand. According to ethereum.org, the fee is paid whether the transaction succeeds or fails.

The MiCA regulation (the EU regulation on markets in crypto-assets) covers e-money tokens, asset-referenced tokens and other crypto-assets, utility tokens among them; according to the European authorities, NFTs in a series or collection may fall within it. According to ESMA (the European Securities and Markets Authority), providers authorised under MiCA are listed in its register: check the provider there. items.d: The web was born at CERN, where Tim Berners-Lee wrote its first proposal in March 1989. According to ethereum.org, Web 1.0 (1990–⁠2004) was mostly static sites that people read; Web 2.0 let everyone publish, but the platform keeps the accounts, the data and the rules. Web3 means applications some of whose records live on a public blockchain: the user holds their own key, and what they own is written in a ledger that no single company keeps. ethereum.org quotes a 2020 line: “Web1 was read-only, Web2 is read-write, Web3 will be read-write-own.” These are labels, not versions: all three exist side by side, and ethereum.org notes that web3 still depends mostly on centralised infrastructure.

items.t: Four promises, and their small print
items.d: Four words keep coming back. Decentralised: no single company runs the network; but NIST, the US standards agency, finds the idea that no one controls a blockchain “not strictly true”. Trustless: according to ethereum.org, the system relies on incentives rather than on an intermediary; NIST points out that you still trust the cryptography, the code, the developers, and the fact that most participants are not secretly colluding. Permissionless: anyone can read, write and produce blocks without asking for approval; this is a property of the software, not a legal permit. Self-sovereign identity: the idea, set out by Christopher Allen in 2016, that a person controls their own digital identity instead of renting it from a platform.

items.d: A ledger is a list of operations, usually kept by a single organisation: NIST points out that you then have to trust it not to lose it, not to change it, not to leave anything out. A distributed ledger is kept by many independent computers, the nodes, and each full node checks everything and keeps its own copy of the ledger (NIST); some software can prune the oldest history (module 6, step 2). The Bitcoin paper (2008) gives the recipe: new operations are broadcast to all nodes, each puts them into a block, and the others accept that block only if everything in it is valid; they show it by building the next block on its fingerprint. A node can leave and come back: it catches up on what it missed. Not all distributed ledgers are public: some are reserved for authorised members (NIST).

items.d: Three tools do almost all the work. A hash function makes a fixed-size fingerprint of any data: the same input always gives the same fingerprint, the slightest change gives another, and you cannot go back from the fingerprint to the data (NIST’s FIPS 180-4 standard). Bitcoin uses SHA-256; Ethereum uses Keccak-256, the original version of Keccak, which gives different results from the final SHA3-256 standard (Ethereum Yellow Paper, FIPS 202). A key pair is a private key kept secret and a public key derived from it: according to ethereum.org, you cannot find the private key from the public one, and an Ethereum address is made of the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 fingerprint of the public key. A signature is made with the private key and anyone can check it with the public key (FIPS 186-5): it proves which key signed and that nothing has changed, but it hides nothing.

items.d: A block has two parts: a small header and a list of operations. In Bitcoin, the header is exactly 80 bytes: a version, the fingerprint of the previous header, a “Merkle root” that sums up all the operations, a date, a difficulty target and a number called the nonce (Bitcoin developer documentation). Because each header contains the fingerprint of the one before, the blocks form a chain: change an old operation and the next link no longer matches. The Merkle tree is built by hashing the operations two by two, then the fingerprints two by two, up to a single root. Its big advantage, according to the Bitcoin paper: a light wallet checks that an operation is in a block with a few fingerprints and the header, without downloading everything.

lab.broken: Broken link: block 1’s fingerprint has changed, block 2 expects the old one.

items.d: Thousands of machines have to choose the next block, and no one decides for them. Proof of work (Bitcoin; Ethereum until 2022): you hash the header again and again, changing the nonce, until you land under a target; finding is expensive, checking takes a single hash (Bitcoin paper). Proof of stake (Ethereum since 15 September 2022): validators stake at least 32 ETH as collateral (up to 2,048 since the Pectra upgrade of May 2025), propose blocks in turn in 12-second slots and vote; cheating can destroy part or all of the deposit (ethereum.org). Delegated proof of stake, for example on TRON: holders elect a small fixed group of producers, 27 according to its documentation. Classic Byzantine consensus, for example CometBFT: a known group of validators votes in rounds and commits a block when more than two thirds agree; it stays safe as long as fewer than a third are faulty.

items.t: The trilemma: two out of three
items.d: The “trilemma” is a rule of thumb, as framed by Vitalik Buterin, co-founder of Ethereum; it is not a proof. It sets three goals: scaling (handling more operations than an ordinary laptop can check), staying decentralised (not depending on a small group of big players), staying secure (holding out even if a large share of the nodes attack). According to him, “simple” techniques get only two: chains where everyone checks everything are secure and decentralised but do not scale; those kept by 10 to 100 nodes are fast and secure but less decentralised; several small chains linked by bridges scale, but each is easier to attack. He argues that more advanced techniques can get all three: that is his argument, not an established fact. The useful question for you: who can still check this chain with an ordinary computer?

items.d: A layer 1 is a base chain, with its own validators and its own consensus: Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana are examples. A layer 2 does the work elsewhere but relies on layer 1 for its security. Rollups execute the operations off the chain, then publish the data to it: “optimistic” rollups assume the batch is correct and leave about seven days to prove fraud; “ZK” rollups publish a mathematical proof that the chain checks, without that wait (ethereum.org). State channels lock funds once on the chain, then the two parties exchange signed updates and only come back when closing; Lightning, on Bitcoin, is an example according to its specifications. A sidechain has its own consensus and a bridge: ethereum.org does not count it as layer 2, because it does not inherit Ethereum’s security.

items.t: Who holds the keys, and are they online?
items.d: A wallet does not contain tokens: it is software or a device that keeps and uses your keys, and the records stay on the chain (ethereum.org). Two questions sort every wallet. Who holds the keys? In a non-custodial wallet, you do: NIST writes that the user is then “fully responsible” for their keys, and that a lost key loses the tokens tied to it. In a custodial wallet, a company keeps them for you: you can recover access, but you trust the company, and a breach on its side can cost you. Is it online? A “hot” wallet is connected and convenient; a “cold” wallet stays offline, and signing takes a physical action (NIST IR 8301).

items.t: Twelve words, a tree of keys
items.d: A recovery phrase is a large random number written as words. The BIP-39 standard takes 128 to 256 random bits, adds a short checksum taken from their SHA-256 fingerprint, cuts the whole into 11-bit pieces, and each piece picks a word from a fixed list of 2,048: you get 12 to 24 words, the last of which partly serves as the check. The words, plus an optional passphrase, go through 2,048 rounds of a function called PBKDF2 to give a “seed”: each different passphrase gives another wallet, also valid. The BIP-32 standard grows a whole tree of keys from that seed: a single backup restores every account, and a single leaked backup gives them all away. Account abstraction (the ERC-4337 standard) takes another path: the account is a smart contract with its own rules, for example recovery by trusted friends and family, without changing Ethereum’s protocol.

items.t: An identifier, a credential, a name
items.d: A decentralised identifier (DID) is a W3C standard from July 2022: a three-part text string, for example did:example:123456789abcdefghi, that points to a document listing the keys that prove who controls this identifier; according to the W3C, many methods use a blockchain, not all. A verifiable credential (W3C standard, version 2.0 of May 2025) is a signed certificate: an issuer, for example a school, signs claims about you, you keep it, and a verifier, for example an employer, checks the signature without calling the school. ENS, Ethereum’s name service, links readable names such as alice.eth to addresses, in two stages: a registry points to a resolver, which answers. None of these tools proves who a person is in the everyday sense: a DID proves control of keys, a name is a label, and facts about a person are worth what their issuer is worth (our reading of the W3C’s roles).

items.d: Our reading of the sources: losses come mostly from a person accepting something, not from broken cryptography. First rule, according to ethereum.org: no service, no support, no legitimate site will ever ask for your recovery phrase. Second rule: know what a signature grants. An “approval” (approve, ERC-20 standard) lets a contract withdraw from your account several times, up to a limit; an unlimited approval stays valid until you revoke it, even after “disconnecting”, and revoking it costs fees (ethereum.org guide). A simple signed message can also set an approval (ERC-2612 standard), and since May 2025 a signature can hand an Ethereum account over to code: the EIP-7702 standard itself says there is “no safe way” for a site to ask for it. Third rule: look before you sign; a wallet can simulate the operation without sending it, which gives a preview, not a guarantee (our reading). Fourth rule, for shared money: a multisig requires m keys out of n, for example 2 out of 3.

items.t: Native asset or token: where does the balance live?
items.d: Each chain has an asset written into its own rules: on Ethereum, ether (ETH). According to ethereum.org, only the protocol creates ether, and it is the only accepted way to pay fees. A token is something else: a balance kept inside a program, a smart contract someone deployed, and its rules (who can create, destroy or freeze it) are written in that program; according to OpenZeppelin, the way tokens are created has to be added by the contract. ETH does not follow the token standard, which is newer than it: applications that only speak that standard go through “wrapped” ETH (WETH), a contract that holds the ETH and issues as many tokens; Solana does the same with wrapped SOL. The real question is not “coin or token?”: is this balance kept by the chain’s rules, or by a program you have to read?

lab.blocked: No ETH to pay the fees: nothing leaves, not even the tokens.
lab.sol: Same principle on Solana: wrapped SOL, with the token program’s “Native Mint”.

a: False: a token follows the rules of its own contract, which you have to read
True: everything on Ethereum follows Ethereum’s rules
items.ok: Yes. ETH is created by the protocol; a token, by its contract (ethereum.org, OpenZeppelin).

no.1: The chain runs the token’s code, but its issuance rules are written by its issuer.
no.2: NFTs too are issued by a contract: the difference is native or contract, not interchangeable or unique.

myth.k: “Coin” and “token” are fixed technical categories.
myth.v: They are words of usage. What you can check: created by the protocol, or kept by a contract. And ETH is not an ERC-20 token (ethereum.org).

items.t: Standards: one socket for every token
items.d: A token standard is a shared list of functions and events, so that wallets and apps can read tokens they have never seen. ERC-20 is Ethereum’s standard for interchangeable tokens: each unit is worth the other, and the contract keeps one balance per address. ERC-721 is the standard for unique tokens (NFTs): each token has its number, and the contract records which address owns each number. ERC-1155 lets a single contract manage several types, interchangeable and unique, and transfer several at once. On Solana, a shared token program keeps one “mint” record per token and one token account per holder. A standard says what the interface looks like, not that a token is useful, safe or honest; and ERC-721 does not store an NFT’s image: it gives a link, optional, that “may” change, according to the standard’s text.

dec.cap: The contract stores an integer; the display depends on decimals.

uri.cap: The number and the owner have not moved; the image shown has. The standard says the link “MAY be mutable”.

lab.same: “From” and “To” are the same address: nothing to transfer.
lab.lowBal: Balance too low: the contract refuses the transfer.
lab.notOwner: This number does not belong to the “From” address: the contract refuses.

a: True, that is the definition of an NFT
Not necessarily: the standard gives a link (tokenURI), optional, which can change
items.ok: Yes. The standard says so: the metadata is optional, and the link can change.

no.0: The standard identifies the NFT by its contract and its number; the image goes through a link.
no.1: Nothing in the Solana documentation cited says the image is in the token.

myth.k: A token that follows a standard is a checked or approved token.
myth.v: A standard is an interface: anyone can deploy a contract that answers balanceOf and transfer. It says nothing about the issuer or the quality of the code.

items.t: How many exist, and who gets them when
items.d: “Tokenomics” are the rules that decide how many units exist, how they appear or disappear, who receives them and when, and what holding them allows. Supply can be capped: Bitcoin’s code halves new issuance every 210,000 blocks, and bitcoin.org writes that only 21 million bitcoins will be created. It can be issued continuously: Ethereum pays its validators in new ETH. Or reduced by destruction: Ethereum burns the base part of every fee, so net supply can go up or down (ethereum.org). For a token, all this is ordinary code: a cap, a creation function, a destruction function, a vesting contract that releases units over time, often after a period when nothing is released (the “cliff”). Voting rights, for their part, often follow the balance, through delegation. Reading these rules is reading rules, not predicting a value.

supply.sum0: Units created up to this height: {u}

no.2: That would be linear vesting without a cliff.

myth.k: A fixed or shrinking supply makes a token go up.
myth.v: Supply rules say how many units exist; they say nothing about demand or value, and this course does not talk about value. A vesting announcement only holds if a contract, which you can read, enforces it.

items.d: A chain that runs programs needs a “virtual machine”: an exact, shared definition of how code runs, so that thousands of computers get the same result from the same data. Ethereum’s, the EVM, is a stack machine that reads small instructions (opcodes) one by one and works on 256-bit numbers; according to ethereum.org, for a given input it produces a deterministic output. Its memory is wiped between transactions; its storage stays. Solana’s engine, called the SVM in Anza’s specification, asks each transaction to declare in advance the accounts it will read and write: those that do not write the same accounts can run in parallel. Move, a language born in 2018 in the Libra project, treats assets as values that cannot be copied or thrown away unless allowed (step 2); CosmWasm runs contracts compiled to WebAssembly on Cosmos SDK chains.

evm.same: Same instructions, same numbers: same result, on every node.
evm.memSay: The memory has been wiped; the storage kept its value.
evm.costs: Costs read from ethereum.org’s table: PUSH1 3, ADD 3, MUL 5.

lanes.say: {t} transactions on {l} lane(s): those that write the same account go one after the other.
lanes.rule: Simplified: two transactions get in each other’s way when one writes an account the other reads or writes.

a: Because a central server sends them the result
Because the EVM is deterministic: same state and same input, same result
Because they vote on the result afterwards
items.ok: Yes. ethereum.org: for a given input, the EVM produces a deterministic output.

no.0: Each client contains its own EVM and runs the code.
no.2: Consensus orders the blocks; the result of running them follows from the rules.

myth.k: A smart contract runs on a computer somewhere, like a web server.
myth.v: Every node that validates the block runs it: that is why it must be deterministic, and why every step costs gas. And EVM code does not run as is on Solana or on CosmWasm.

items.d: Contract languages compile to virtual machine instructions. On the EVM, Solidity is, according to ethereum.org, a curly-bracket language influenced mostly by C++, statically typed; Vyper is a Python-like language that deliberately has fewer features than Solidity, to make contracts safer and easier to audit. Its documentation lists what it does not offer, including modifiers, class inheritance, inline assembly, recursion and infinite loops; recursion and infinite loops are left out because they make it impossible to bound gas. On Solana, the token program is written in Rust, and the Anchor framework is used to write programs; CosmWasm contracts are also written in Rust. In Move, a value without the copy “ability” simply cannot be duplicated. A language does not make a contract safe on its own: it changes which mistakes are easy or hard to make.

vy.gas: Left out by choice: it would make it impossible to set a gas ceiling.
vy.read: Left out by choice: Vyper’s goals are security, simplicity of the language and the compiler, and human-readable code.

bound.infSay: Maximum gas: ∞, impossible to bound. That is the reason Vyper gives.

can be put inside another value

move.dropOk: Thrown away: the drop ability allows it.

items.q: Vyper has neither class inheritance nor modifiers. Why?
a: Because it is an unfinished language
Because the EVM does not allow inheritance
By choice, for code that is easier to read and to audit
items.ok: Yes. According to ethereum.org and its own documentation, Vyper deliberately has fewer features, for security and auditing.

no.0: Its documentation presents these absences as a choice.
no.1: Vyper explains these absences by its own goals; it is not a limit of the machine.

myth.k: Pick the “safe” language, and the contract is safe.
myth.v: A language removes certain mistakes; logic errors, wrong permissions and false assumptions remain (module 9). And Solidity is not “the JavaScript of blockchains”: ethereum.org says it is influenced mostly by C++, and statically typed.

items.t: From draft to the real network
items.d: A developer almost never sends a contract straight to a real network. They write it, compile it, test it on a fake chain running on their computer, try it on a public test network, and only then deploy it for real. Hardhat and Foundry, for example, are environments that compile, test and deploy; Foundry brings together Forge (compile, test, deploy), Cast (command line), Anvil (a local node) and Chisel (a Solidity console). Remix runs in the browser with no installation, with a sandbox chain and ten made-up accounts each loaded with 100 made-up ETH. OpenZeppelin Contracts is a library of community-checked building blocks, to be used as installed, without copying or changing them, according to its own documentation. Tools change often; for you, the order is what counts: local tests, public test network, review, then main network.

myth.v: They are trial values with no link to the main network; be wary of anyone selling them (step 6 of the buyer path). And using OpenZeppelin does not mean the contract is audited: the library is checked, not the project’s code around it.

items.t: Gas, or the price of each instruction
items.d: Every instruction a contract runs costs an amount of “gas”, a unit of work: according to ethereum.org, adding costs 3, and a simple ETH transfer uses 21,000; according to the EIP-2929 standard, reading a storage slot for the first time in a transaction costs 2,100, then 100. The fee is the gas used multiplied by a price per unit, and since EIP-1559 (August 2021) that price has two parts: a base fee set by the network and burnt, and a tip that goes to the block producer. The base fee moves by at most 12.5 % per block: it rises when blocks are more than half full, falls otherwise. You set a maximum; what is not used is returned. If a transaction runs out of gas, its changes are undone, but the gas provided is consumed (ethereum.org). Optimising means getting the same result with cheaper instructions, for example reading a value once and keeping it, or declaring it constant.

fee.under: The max fee is below the base fee: the transaction cannot get into this block.
fee.gwei: A gwei is a billionth of an ETH. No money prices here.

v: 0 gas of storage reads: the compiler does not reserve a slot for it (Solidity)
opt.cap: Read costs only; memory and the surrounding execution are not counted here.

dry.say: Gas limit too low: changes undone, and the gas provided is consumed.

items.q: Your transaction runs out of gas. What happens?
a: Nothing is done and nothing is paid
It waits for you to add gas
The changes are undone, but the gas used is paid
items.ok: Yes. ethereum.org: the EVM undoes the changes, but all the gas provided is consumed.

no.0: The gas used is paid.
no.1: The changes are undone; a new transaction would be needed.

myth.k: Gas is a fee the app or the wallet chooses.
myth.v: It is the network’s measure of work: the base fee is set by the protocol and burnt, the tip goes to the block producer. A failed transaction is not free, and a high maximum is not paid in full: the rest is returned.

items.t: The site, the library, the wallet
items.d: What is new in a dApp is that its JavaScript talks to the chain through a library, and to the visitor’s wallet through a shared interface. Browser wallets expose an object defined by the EIP-1193 standard: the site calls request(…), the wallet answers, or refuses with error 4001, “User Rejected Request”. Libraries such as ethers.js or Viem, for example, wrap this: ethers separates a read-only “Provider” from a “Signer” that acts for an account; Viem separates a public client (read) from a wallet client (send, sign). Wagmi is a library of React “hooks” built on Viem. WalletConnect links a site to a wallet on another device, through a QR code or a link, with encrypted messages. To remember: reading the chain needs no wallet; only signing does, and it is the wallet, not the site, that holds the keys and asks you.

items.t: The node: who answers when the site asks
items.d: A node is a computer running the chain’s software: it downloads the blocks, checks them and keeps the current state. Sites and wallets ask it questions through a standard interface, JSON-RPC: “what is the latest block?”, “what is this address’s balance?”. According to ethereum.org, a full node checks every block but keeps only recent state, usually the last 128 blocks; an archive node keeps everything since the start, which runs to terabytes; a light node downloads only the headers. Running your own node means checking for yourself, without revealing to a third party the addresses you look up. Many apps go through node-as-a-service companies: ethereum.org lists about thirty, including Alchemy, Infura and QuickNode, and notes that you then centralise that part of the product. For your project, “through which node do we read, and what happens when it goes down?” is a design question.

who.prov: The provider sees the address requested, and your site depends on it.

Nothing changes: the data is in the browser

no.2: The browser asks a node every time.

myth.k: A node provider is “the blockchain”.
myth.v: They are one company’s nodes answering for you; any node can check the data. And not every node answers old questions: that takes an archive node.

items.t: Files: a fingerprint and a keeper
items.d: A blockchain is a bad place for files: according to ethereum.org, every node would have to store everything, and the fees would make it prohibitive. So you usually keep a short fingerprint on the chain, and the file elsewhere. IPFS finds a file by what it contains, not by where it is: its address, the CID, is built from its fingerprint, so the slightest change gives another CID. But IPFS promises to keep nothing: according to its documentation, a file stays available as long as a node keeps it (“pins” it), and the rest can be deleted to make room. Filecoin adds payment: storage providers lock up collateral and must prove every day that they still have the data. Arweave presents itself as “pay once, store forever”: that is its promise, according to its documentation, not a fact about the future.

items.d: Two problems live at the edge of every application on a chain. The first: a chain is made for writing and checking, not for searching; The Graph, for example, says so, and without an index a question means going through the chain block by block. An indexer reads the events once and files them in a database you can query; at The Graph, a “subgraph” describes which contracts and which events to index. The second: according to ethereum.org, a contract has no access by default to information off the chain. An oracle brings it in, and brings trust back: even a “reputable” provider can cheat or be hacked. Chainlink, for example, updates a value when it drifts beyond a threshold or when a delay (“heartbeat”) has passed; Pyth, for example, lets the application fetch a signed value, with a confidence interval, and recommends refusing a value that is too old. In every case, the contract must check whether the data is fresh and sound.

items.d: A decentralised exchange (DEX) is a program that swaps one token for another without a company holding the funds. An order book lists offers by price and matches them, like a stock exchange; some chains, for example dYdX according to its documentation, keep that book in their nodes. An automated market maker (AMM) has no offers: it keeps a pool of two tokens, and a formula sets the price; in the best known, described by Uniswap, the product of the two balances must not fall (x × y = k), so a large trade moves the price more. Slippage is the gap between the price seen and the price obtained; a tolerance you set cancels the trade beyond it. Those who deposit both tokens earn fees, but if the price moves they can end up with less than if they had kept their tokens: that is “impermanent loss” (Uniswap).

items.d: A lending protocol is a shared pool: some deposit, others borrow. With no credit check, the borrower first deposits collateral worth more than the loan. The protocol watches a number, called the health factor at Aave for example: the value of the collateral, reduced by a threshold set for each asset, divided by what is owed. If it drops below 1, anyone can repay part of the debt and take part of the collateral at a discount: that is a liquidation, done by bots racing each other (Aave). Rates are not negotiated: a formula raises them as more of the pool is borrowed. A flash loan is taken with no collateral, on condition that it is repaid, with fees, before the end of the same transaction; otherwise everything is undone. Attackers use them too (module 9).

hf.liq: A liquidator repays part of the debt and takes part of the collateral.

items.d: A stablecoin is a token designed to track a stable value, usually the US dollar. What holds it to that value, and whom do you have to trust? According to ethereum.org, a fiat-backed stablecoin is issued by a company that says it keeps reserves and redeems 1 for 1: you trust the company and its audits. A crypto-backed stablecoin is created by contracts against deposits worth more than the tokens issued; if the collateral falls too fast, it is liquidated. An algorithmic stablecoin is not backed by any other asset and holds its value through rules that create or destroy tokens: according to ethereum.org, you then have to trust the algorithm, or be able to read it. According to a complaint by the SEC (the US markets authority), TerraUSD, an algorithmic stablecoin, lost its peg in May 2022 and fell close to zero.

items.d: A “yield” always comes from somewhere: where? Staking, in proof of stake, means locking the native asset to run a validator: the protocol rewards good work and destroys part or all of the deposit for proven cheating (ethereum.org). Liquid staking hands the deposit to a service that gives a receipt, a token; according to ethereum.org, the protocol does not know that token, and you also depend on the service (contracts, operators, governance). Restaking commits an already locked deposit to secure other services, with other penalties: the risks stack up (ethereum.org). A yield aggregator is a vault that, in our reading, places deposits in other protocols; the ERC-4626 standard, which mentions aggregators, describes these vaults in “shares”. Perpetual contracts let you bet on a price going up or down with no expiry; to stay close to the reference price, one side regularly pays the other.

items.t: From the vote to the transfer
items.d: In a DAO, point to three things: where people vote, where the money is, and who or what carries out the decision. Off-chain voting means signing a message with your wallet, with no fees and no transaction, and a service counts the signatures; Snapshot, for example, works this way, and freezes voting power at a given block so that no one votes twice by moving their tokens. But this vote moves nothing: someone still has to carry it out. On-chain voting is a transaction to a “Governor” contract; if the proposal passes, it can execute it, often after a delay (timelock) which, according to OpenZeppelin, lets those who disagree leave. The treasury is often in a multisignature account, for example Safe: it only sends funds once a set number of its owners have confirmed, say 3 of 5. “The DAO voted” and “the money moved” are two events, and the trust sits in the second.

myth.v: Most real set-ups have people at the execution stage (signers, the delay’s administrator, a guardian), and that is where the trust sits. Off-chain voting is not false for all that: it can be checked, it simply executes nothing.

items.d: The simplest rule: one token, one vote; whoever holds more tokens weighs more. Delegation lets you lend your voting power to someone who follows the proposals, like a representative (ethereum.org); on some contracts you even have to delegate to yourself for your tokens to count (OpenZeppelin). Quadratic voting lets you show how much you care about a question without the richest winning everything: n votes cost n² credits, so each extra vote costs more than the one before, and ten votes cost a hundred credits. Vitalik Buterin points out that it only works if one person cannot easily create many accounts. “Soulbound” governance is the idea of granting the vote through non-transferable tokens, tied to participation rather than to money: it is a proposal, with a minimal standard (ERC-5192), not a proven system.

items.t: The law does not disappear with code
items.d: Code does not make a group invisible to the law. In the United States, in the Ooki DAO case, a court held that a DAO was a “person” under the commodity markets law and fined it, according to the CFTC, the US authority for those markets. A “legal wrapper” is an ordinary form in which the DAO registers, to sign contracts, pay people and limit its members’ liability: Wyoming created the “DAO LLC” in 2021, and a decentralised unincorporated nonprofit association (DUNA) in 2024, with at least 100 members. Paying contributors raises the questions of any organisation; tax and employment law depend on the country: ask an accountant or a lawyer. “Progressive decentralisation” is a guide written by an investor (a16z, 2020), not a law: start as a team, then hand over control in stages.

items.d: The same mistakes keep coming back (our reading of the Solidity and ethereum.org guides). Reentrancy: a contract that pays before updating its books can be called again and pay again; according to ethereum.org, that is how in 2016 about 3.6 million ETH left “The DAO”; the fix, according to Solidity: update first, pay afterwards. Overflow: before Solidity 0.8.0, a calculation past the maximum started again from zero, and below zero started again from the maximum, with no error; since then, the operation is reverted by default, except in an “unchecked” block. Transaction ordering (MEV): whoever orders the block sees the pending transactions and can slip their own in just before and after yours, a “sandwich”. The manipulated oracle: a price read from a single pool can be pushed for the length of a transaction, with a flash loan. Access control: an admin function open to everyone, or one key with every power.

items.d: Because a deployed contract is hard to change, security is done in layers, each catching part of what slipped past the one before. Unit tests check each function on chosen examples. Fuzzing throws many random inputs and reports when a rule is broken; Foundry, for example, runs 256 tries per test by default. Static analysis reads the code without running it and spots known patterns, such as reentrancy; Slither, for example, is a free tool that runs a set of detectors. Formal verification proves that the code respects rules written in mathematics, but only proves what the rules say. Audits are reviews by outside experts, and bug bounties pay those who report a flaw instead of exploiting it; according to ethereum.org, an audit does not find every bug. No layer is a guarantee.

items.d: To move a token or a message from one chain to another, you need a bridge. The common design, “lock then mint”, locks the token in a contract on chain A, and a contract on B creates a token that represents it (ethereum.org). Everything depends on who tells B that the locking happened. In a “trusted” bridge, an outside group signs that message: if enough of its keys are stolen, fake messages drain the locked funds. A light-client bridge, of which IBC is an example according to ethereum.org, lets B check A itself: no new group to trust in that mode, but it is harder to build. LayerZero, for example, lets each application choose its verifiers; Chainlink CCIP relies by default on a committee of independent operators, and lets you require others (according to their documentation). According to ethereum.org, bridges account for the three biggest DeFi hacks.

items.d: The browser sends a request with a method, an address and headers. The server returns a status and often a body; according to MDN, the web’s reference documentation, statuses fall into five classes, from 100 to 599. The interface translates those results into states a person understands.

pick.v: The request has gone and nothing has come back: a waiting state that does not block the page.
A 200 with an empty list is a success. The screen says “No workshops yet”, not “error”.
A 200 with workshops: the list renders.
A 500, or no answer: a separate message and a way to retry. According to MDN, a 503 means the server is temporarily unavailable.

items.ex: A workshop page requests an event list. A valid empty list should render a helpful empty state. An unexpected server error needs a separate message.
items.try: Draw loading, empty, success and error versions of the event list. Match each version to a network condition.
items.check: An empty 200 response becomes an empty state. A failed request becomes an error state with a way to retry where appropriate.
items.q: The workshop list comes back empty, with a 200 status. The screen shows…
a: a helpful empty state: “No workshops yet”
items.ok: Yes. An empty 200 is a success: say there is nothing, not that it failed.

items.h: Make the data tell the truth.
items.d: Give each entity a stable identifier, link them with foreign keys, and let the database enforce what it can enforce. Keep the display name separate from the identifier. That is our workshop’s method.

pick.v: id · name. A room hosts several workshops.
id · title · capacity · room_id. The title may change, the identifier never.
id · workshop_id · name · state. It points to the workshop’s identifier, not to its title.

items.ex: Workshop records have an ID and a capacity. Booking records reference the workshop ID. A renamed workshop keeps its existing bookings.
items.try: Sketch a schema for a room that hosts several events and an event that accepts many bookings.
items.check: Room, workshop, booking: two one-to-many relationships. The booking stores workshop_id, so it stays attached when the workshop title changes.
items.q: A workshop changes its title. Its bookings…
items.ok: Yes. Link by identifier, never by the display name.

items.d: A contract states the accepted input and the response for each meaningful outcome. Validate on the server and give clients stable error identifiers. Run three possible requests: the server’s response changes the interface.

see: “That workshop is full. See other dates.”
lab.src: According to MDN: 201, the request succeeded and a new resource was created; 400, the server will not process a request perceived as a client error; 409, the request conflicts with the current state of the server.

items.ex: POST /bookings accepts a workshop identifier and a name. A successful creation, malformed input and a full workshop need distinct handling.
items.try: Write three response examples and the corresponding interface treatment.
items.check: A success shows the reservation. Invalid input focuses the relevant field. A capacity conflict explains what happened and leaves the person able to browse other times.
items.q: No seats are left. The server answers…
a: 409 Conflict, and the screen offers other dates
items.ok: Yes. The conflict is said, and the person keeps a way out.

items.d: According to the PostgreSQL documentation, a transaction bundles multiple steps into a single, all-or-nothing operation. Concurrent requests still need a rule: SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the workshop’s row, and other transactions that want it wait until the first one ends. That only holds if every write path follows the same rule.

pick.v: BEGIN: the transaction opens. Its changes stay invisible to others until it commits.
SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the workshop’s row: the second request waits here.
Read the remaining seats again, now that nobody else can change them.
INSERT then COMMIT, or ROLLBACK: the booking exists in full, or not at all.

items.ex: Two people request the final seat. Both requests reach the API. One locks the workshop, confirms capacity and commits. The second checks capacity after it acquires the lock.
items.try: Write a test that sends two booking requests for one remaining seat. Run it against a local database.
items.check: Exactly one new booking commits; the other request returns a capacity conflict. Repeating a completed request with the same idempotency key follows the documented replay behaviour.
items.q: Two people ask for the last seat at the same moment. With the row lock…
a: only one goes through; the other gets a capacity conflict
items.ok: Yes. The second waits for the lock, reads again, and finds the workshop full.

items.d: Authentication establishes identity. Authorization checks whether that identity can perform the current operation on the specific resource. Our rule: that check runs on the server, on every request.

pick.v: Sees the public workshops. Sees no bookings.
Sees public data and their own bookings, not anyone else’s.
Edits their own workshops, not another organizer’s.

items.ex: A signed-in organizer can edit their own workshop. A participant only sees their own booking details and public event data.
items.try: Make a permission matrix for anonymous visitors, participants and organizers. Turn each cell into a test case.
items.check: Include an organizer trying to edit a different organizer’s event. A valid session alone does not grant permission for that record.
items.q: A signed-in organizer tries to edit someone else’s workshop. The server…
a: declines: their session gives them no right on that workshop
items.ok: Yes. Being signed in says who you are, not what you may do.

items.h: Ship a release you can diagnose.
items.d: A release needs a known configuration, a repeatable build, a smoke test and a rollback plan. Logs should help explain requests without collecting secrets or unnecessary private data. That is our workshop’s list.

pick.v: Run the checks: nothing ships if one fails.
The smoke test: the workshop list and one test booking.
Release a known version, by its commit identifier.
Verify, and roll back if needed, following each failure by its request ID.

items.ex: Deploy the booking flow to staging. Check the event list and one test booking, validate database changes and correlate failures by request ID.
items.try: Write a pre-release checklist and demonstrate a rollback on a disposable staging deployment.
items.check: Record the working build, expected migration state and smoke-test results. Confirm the previous build remains compatible with the database or prepare a tested recovery plan.
items.q: Before releasing, what do you keep at hand?
a: nothing: we will fix it live
the working build, the expected database state and a tested rollback
items.ok: Yes. A version you can put back beats a fix made live.

all.d: The build is stamped. Next is yours: the Studio builds custom web applications.
