w3.lead: For builders: prototype a verifiable attendance receipt on a development network (ethereum.org: a chain designed for local development), with synthetic data. This is education, not an offer.
w3.tabs: The six lessons of the local chain

items.d: A public chain can let independent parties inspect a shared record. It also adds visibility, cost and operational complexity. Our workshop rule: ordinary application data stays in the database, and only the minimum to verify goes on the chain.

pick.v: Bookings and contacts: names, email addresses, guest lists.
A public receipt identifier, nothing personal.
Reads the proof and its status, writes nothing.

items.ex: Attendance receipts could be independently verified. Names, email addresses, guest lists and support notes stay in the booking system.
items.try: List the data you need for a proof. Remove anything that could identify a person without their consent.
items.check: Only the minimum public reference goes on the chain. No email address, and nothing guessed from one.
items.q: What goes on the chain for an attendance receipt?
a: a public receipt identifier, nothing personal
items.ok: Yes. The minimum to verify; the rest stays in the database.

items.h: Read what the wallet is asking.
items.d: A wallet helps people manage signing; a signature authorizes a specific payload under an account key. Connecting, signing a message and signing a transaction are three different actions; ethereum.org calls a transaction a cryptographically signed instruction from an account.

pick.v: The site reads the public address chosen: ethereum.org says it is like a login you can use across many apps.
The screen shows the intended action and the network, before any request.
The person approves this request, and nothing else.
The site checks the result and the network used.

items.ex: The receipt demo reads a wallet address for a local exercise. It requests a write only when the learner explicitly chooses to issue a demo receipt.
items.try: Sketch separate screens for connection, review, approval and cancellation. Use a fresh development wallet, on the local chain.
items.check: The review shows the intended action and network. A declined request leaves the interface usable. The app never asks for a recovery phrase or a private key.
items.q: An app asks for your recovery phrase to “verify” your wallet. That is…
a: a warning sign: never give it
items.ok: Yes. Whoever has the phrase has the wallet: give it to no one.

items.h: Show the difference between a read and a submission.
items.d: ethereum.org’s JSON-RPC documentation: a read (eth_call) runs without creating a transaction on the chain. A write follows a transaction’s life: sending returns its identifier (the hash), and the receipt, which says success or failure, is not available while the transaction is pending. Follow a receipt, state by state.

do: Read the receipt and the state
chain: A receipt with status “success”, under the demo’s rule
lab.src: ethereum.org, JSON-RPC API: the receipt is not available for pending transactions, and its status is 1 (success) or 0 (failure).

items.ex: Read whether a receipt ID exists. When issuing one, show the demo transaction hash and update the status after checking the receipt.
items.try: Design status screens for awaiting approval, submitted, failed and confirmed.
items.check: A hash alone means the action was submitted. The confirmed view relies on a successful receipt and the confirmation rule chosen for the demo.
items.q: Right after sending, the site shows the transaction hash. The operation is…
a: sent, not confirmed yet: it needs the receipt
items.ok: Yes. The hash says “sent”. The receipt says whether it worked.

items.h: Turn the contract into explicit rules.
items.d: A smart contract is code deployed to a network; ethereum.org notes that deployed contract code usually cannot be changed to patch security flaws. Our method: define who may act, what changes and what is announced before wiring a front end, then test the intended and the rejected actions locally.

pick.v: One authorized account issues the demo receipts.
A receipt ID is used only once.
The contract stores the new ID.
A successful issue announces the receipt reference.

items.ex: Only the demo issuer may record a synthetic attendance ID. Duplicate IDs are rejected. A successful issue emits an event.
items.try: Write local tests for issuance, duplicate rejection and an unauthorized account, with synthetic IDs.
items.check: A valid call creates one receipt. Invalid calls create none and leave prior state intact.
items.q: An unauthorized account tries to issue a receipt. The contract…
a: refuses, and the state stays as it was
items.ok: Yes. A refused action leaves no trace in the state.

items.h: Build a useful timeline from events.
items.d: Contract events can feed an application index. Our workshop method: keep the chain and the event’s position with each indexed row, make processing repeatable, and plan for the latest blocks being reorganized, under the chosen chain’s own rule.

pick.v: The contract emits it.
Reads a range of blocks.
Inserts or updates the event’s row.
Shows the indexed state.

items.ex: A receipt page shows a searchable list of demo issuance events. The indexer records the latest processed block and can rebuild the view.
items.try: Replay the same batch twice, then simulate dropping a recent block from the source history.
items.check: The second run creates no duplicates. Rebuilt data matches the history kept after the simulated change.
items.q: The same batch of events is replayed twice. The index…
a: stays the same: one row per event
items.ok: Yes. A repeatable process gives the same index on every run.

items.h: Keep the booking app useful without a wallet.
items.d: Build the normal experience first, then a separate proof-verification path with clear failure states. Our rule: the proof degrades gracefully when the node is down; ethereum.org notes that an app must connect to a node to read the chain.

pick.v: An off-chain record, in the database.
The local-chain demo.
A read-only proof lookup.
The result, and its limits.

items.ex: A workshop organizer issues demo receipts locally. A visitor books without a wallet and can verify an anonymized receipt later.
items.try: Demo the full flow, then disconnect the node. Show the booking flow and the verification state during the outage.
items.check: Booking still works. Verification says the network is unavailable and never claims a proof was checked.
items.q: The node stops answering. The visitor…
a: books anyway; verification says it is unavailable
items.ok: Yes. The proof is an extra; the booking does not depend on it.

all.d: The receipt is stamped. On the client’s side, the Bookshop’s web3 course helps decide whether a chain is needed; we build the ordinary route.

calc.t: The sum, with your own numbers
calc.brief: The starting figures are the lesson’s. Change one: the result follows, and the exercise is done. Nothing is sent.

fiche.brief: Answer for yourself: each answer fills its box of the brief, on this device only. One answer is enough to do the exercise; nothing is required.

shelf.name: The Lantern Bookshop
shelf.heroK: / THE BOOKSHOP · THE WORLD OF NUMIDEA
shelf.lore: The Lantern is a night bookshop in the world of Numidea. The workshop crew built the booking for its night class here; the bookseller kept their field notebooks, and they became atlases. Each atlas is a course: you pick a district, settle a situation, do the exercise, and the decision goes into the case journal. The lessons are free; the keepsakes are earned. Nothing leaves here until you press.

shelf.passLead: The keepsakes earned in every atlas, together. They stay in this browser.

home.name: Home
home.alt: Numidea Labs poster “HOME · YASSER & KURO”: Yasser standing in the workshop among a lamp, books and plans; Kūro on a pile of books, a second cat asleep, a pigeon, a raven and a rat.
home.lore: An envelope from Lantern Bookshop lands at the Argent Workshop. Its owner is opening a night printmaking class and is tired of counting seats in messages. Kūro settles on the only slip that matters: the date of the first class.
home.rule: A project brief can start with one problem, one person, and one result.
home.q: Lantern’s owner asks for “something digital” before the first night class. Where should Yasser start?
a: Ask where a customer gets stuck.
List every feature a competitor has.
f: A logo might help. First find out whether the friction is recognition, information, or the way an order gets handled.
Start with a recent example and an outcome you can observe. The right tool comes after that.
A feature list skips the person who needs to use it. Ask about a real visit or order first.
home.handoff: Start with a first class, limited seats, and bookings buried in messages.
home.decision: Brief agreed: visitors should see the session details and reserve one seat without messaging.

ex.brief: Match the visitor’s task, their difficulty and the result we want to observe.
choices: Check the session date and price
A visitor must message to confirm a seat
ex.empty: Fill all three parts. A useful brief names the task, where it gets hard, and how you’ll know it improved.
ex.ok: A visitor needs the date and price, but must message to confirm a seat. We’ll test whether they can book straight from the event page.
ex.bad: Match the event you can observe at the end to the result. The friction is what interrupts the task today.

fields.name: Fields
fields.alt: Poster “FIELDS · YASSER & THE CREW”: Yasser in a field of tall grass, a raven on his shoulder, a pigeon in flight; at his feet Kūro, another cat and a rat among books and maps.
fields.lore: Pigeon takes the brief to Lantern and watches two people try to join the night class. Their routes differ. Both stop before choosing a seat.
fields.rule: Discovery turns a guess into a testable observation.
fields.q: You suspect visitors leave because the class date or price is hard to find. What can you collect first?
a: Count how many colors are on the homepage.
Rewrite the event page before watching anyone.
Watch two people try to find the class date and price.
f: Color is easy to count, but it won’t tell you if someone found the session details.
A rewrite could bury the same information again. Find where the user expects it first.
Observe where they look and what they ask. This gives you a concrete place to investigate.
fields.scene: Two routes to the same stall
fields.handoff: Carry the brief into two observed visits.
fields.decision: Field evidence: put the class date and price beside the booking action.

ex.brief: Watch two customers before deciding what needs to move.
ex.obsPhone: Phone visitor opens the class page, scrolls past the poster, and looks for the date in the footer.
ex.obsDesk: Desktop visitor finds the date but opens a message window to ask for the price and seat availability.
ex.one: One observation helps you form a question. Watch the other visit before making a decision.
ex.ok: Both visitors wanted class details before committing. Test putting the date and price beside Book.

audience.name: Audience
audience.alt: Poster “AUDIENCE”: Yasser in profile, surrounded by hands holding out icons (“research”, “trust”, “accessibility”, “experience”); at his feet Kūro, a raven, a pigeon and a rat.
audience.lore: Pigeon’s field notes put the date and price above the booking button. At the Listening District, Kūro shadows a visitor testing the new form without a mouse.
audience.rule: A path works when the people who need it can complete it.
audience.q: Lantern’s new form works with a mouse. A keyboard user can’t tell where they are. What changes?
a: Add visible focus and walk the form with Tab.
Make the submit button larger only.
f: Check every field, action and error message in order. You can observe exactly where the journey breaks.
It won’t tell them which control has focus.
Size helps some users. They still need a visible focus state throughout the form.
audience.handoff: Use the new event layout and test it from the first control to Book.
audience.decision: Access check: visible focus follows the booking order through the entire form.

ex.brief: Follow the booking form one control at a time and see why focus visibility matters.
ex.enabled: Focus is now visible. Step through the controls to check their order.
ex.hidden: Focus moved, but the visitor cannot see which control is active. Enable a visible indicator.
ex.ok: All fields reached in order. The visitor can see where they are and reach Book.

identity.name: Identity
identity.alt: Poster “IDENTITY”: Yasser among the pieces of an identity (“LOGO”, “TYPE”, “VOICE”, “SYSTEM”), Kūro at his feet, a mug and four other characters.
identity.lore: Yasser draws a folded-book mark for Lantern. It has to feel like the shop on the window, the event page, and the tiny tab a visitor returns to after comparing dates.
identity.rule: Make the identity usable across surfaces with a consistent family of marks.
identity.q: The sign reads well, but the logo turns into a blob in a tiny browser tab. Which asset belongs there?
a: The full wordmark and the tagline.
A compact mark with the same outer shape.
f: The details compete at small size. Keep them for placements with enough space.
It might read, but it loses the connection to the identity the visitor already recognises.
A deliberate small version keeps the strongest cues and drops detail that cannot survive at that size.
identity.scene: A mark for the shop and the tab
identity.handoff: Carry the recognisable bookshop shape into the usable booking flow.
identity.decision: Design proof: keep the folded-book silhouette at favicon size.

ex.brief: Shrink two versions of a fictional book mark. Compare what you can still recognize.
ex.hint: Slide toward 16 pixels and watch what happens to the inner lines.
ex.ok: At favicon size, the compact version keeps the visible book shape. The detailed version loses its fine lines.

architecture.name: Architecture
architecture.alt: Poster “ARCHITECTURE”: Yasser leaning on a giant pencil in the middle of a maze (“backend”, “logic”, “automation”, “structure”); a raven, a pigeon, Kūro and a rat.
architecture.lore: Ratman follows the booking form’s copper line to the relay. The page is ready to take bookings. The relay still has to decide who gets the last seat.
architecture.rule: The server must handle contention for a limited resource before it confirms a booking.
architecture.q: Two customers request the last seat at the same time. Which system should decide who gets it?
a: Confirm both and send a correction later.
The server checks and updates capacity as one protected operation.
Each browser checks its copy of the seat count.
f: That pushes a preventable conflict onto the customers.
Only one request should complete the reservation. The other receives a clear “full” response.
Both browsers might have the same stale count. The decision needs one authoritative write path.
architecture.handoff: Connect the booking form and its capacity relay.
architecture.decision: Relay rule: check and reserve the last seat in one protected server operation.

ex.brief: Run the same two requests through competing capacity rules. See what each visitor gets.
ex.bothMsg: Oversold. Both browsers saw the same old seat count and issued a confirmation.
ex.oneMsg: Exactly one seat was booked. A single protected operation checks capacity and records the booking before confirmation.
ex.more: Run the other rule too, to compare.

launch.name: Launch
launch.alt: Poster “LAUNCH”: Yasser mid-leap through orange flames (“deploy”, “ship”, “release”, “iterate”); below, a raven, a pigeon, Kūro, a rat and a mug.
launch.lore: Pigeon carries Lantern’s new site to the Logistics Yard. The booking relay passed its capacity test. Now a staging run has to make it all the way to the confirmation.
launch.rule: Test a release and keep a known recovery path.
launch.q: Lantern is about to publish its new booking flow. What is the best final rehearsal?
a: Place a test booking on staging and confirm the rollback plan.
Open the event page and stop when it loads.
Release and wait for customer messages.
f: Check the meaningful task end to end and know what you will restore if the new release fails.
Loading is useful. It doesn’t tell you if a visitor can reserve a seat and see a confirmation.
Run the core journey yourself while the recovery path is still easy to use.
launch.handoff: Carry the working relay into staging and test the complete booking.
launch.decision: Release decision: keep the working build live until the staging confirmation passes.

ex.brief: Make a staging booking, then decide what to do about the failing release.
ex.r0: Live: previous release · Staging: new release
ex.r1: Staging: booking confirmation fails · Live: previous release
ex.stageMsg: The homepage loads, but the booking fails at confirmation. The exercise begins with the previous release still available.
ex.promoteMsg: Customers now reach a broken order flow. Restore the last working release.
ex.keepB: Keep or restore last working release
ex.keepEarly: You protected the live path. Run a staging booking to see what would have failed.
ex.ok: Live bookings work while you repair the staging build. Re-run the full booking before promoting it.

growth.name: Growth
growth.alt: Poster “GROWTH”: Yasser surrounded by cards (“SEO”, “ANALYTICS”, “CONTENT”, “OPTIMIZATION”) and the crew legend in hand lettering (“KURO”, “RAVEN”, “PIGEON”, “RAT”); all four at the foot of the plinth.
growth.lore: Lantern opens the booking page after the confirmation fix. Raven watches 100 fictional visits. Only 40 people reach the form, which brings Pigeon’s field notes back into focus.
growth.rule: Choose a signal that reflects the task you are improving.
growth.q: More people visit the booking page, but completed bookings barely change. What do you compare?
a: Visits to the page versus completed bookings.
The total likes on the launch post.
The number of posts you wrote.
f: Compare the share that finishes, then inspect the biggest drop-off step before changing it.
Attention can grow without the booking journey improving.
That describes your output, not whether visitors could book.
growth.handoff: After the confirmation fix, compare the live booking stages.
growth.decision: Growth lead: 60 of 100 visits stopped before the form. Test whether the date, price, and booking action are clear.

ex.brief: Inspect a fictional booking funnel. Which step loses the most people?
rows: Visitors
Started booking
Booked
tips: Every person who reached the page.
60 of 100 did not start. Check whether the offer and the next action are clear.
8 of 40 did not complete. That’s a smaller loss than the 60 visitors lost before the form.

observer.name: Observer
observer.alt: Poster “01 / THE OBSERVER · THE NEUTRAL EYE”: a large open eye in the night sky, above a figure in a red coat on a hill.
observer.lore: After the class, a visitor asks for a receipt that someone else can verify. Raven opens a window in the Observatory. The attendee list stays in Lantern’s locked drawer.
observer.rule: Separate public verification from private customer records. This simulation uses fictional receipts.
observer.q: A visitor wants to verify an attendance receipt publicly. What belongs in that record?
a: A crowd photo and the whole list of attendees.
f: That publishes much more than the verifier needs.
Those details are unnecessary for this proof and can reveal private information.
The public lookup can answer whether the demo issuer recorded the receipt. Contact details stay in the booking system.
observer.scene: A window and a locked drawer
observer.handoff: Create an optional receipt lookup after attendance.
observer.decision: Proof boundary: publish only an opaque receipt reference. Keep attendee details private.

ex.brief: Choose which fields the fictional public archive can see. Run a receipt lookup with your choices.
ex.pickMsg: Select what should be visible, then run the lookup.
ex.none: Lookup can’t work without a public receipt reference.
ex.ok: Receipt found. The verifier can check the reference while customer details stay private.
ex.over: The archive would expose details it doesn’t need. Keep only the opaque receipt ID public.

wire.name: Moonlit Wire
wire.alt: MERCURY poster: the traveller in a red coat walks a power line under the full moon, Kūro follows on the wire, the town and its arches below.
wire.lore: Kūro follows Raven out into MERCURY. The crossing is a rehearsal for Lantern’s new receipt screen. Each stepping point offers one action and one visible result.
wire.rule: A complex flow becomes easier when the next safe step is clear.
wire.q: A visitor opens Lantern’s receipt screen for the first time. What should it make easy?
a: Complete one real task and see a clear result.
f: A visual choice can wait until the visitor understands the task.
Give the visitor a short successful path. They can discover advanced controls after they know what the tool does.
That gives a beginner more decisions without a reason to make them.
wire.handoff: Rehearse the receipt screen with Kūro, one meaningful step at a time.
wire.decision: Wayfinding rule: one clear action, followed by a result the visitor can see.

ex.brief: Advance Kūro by giving him a clear next step. There is no timer.
msgs: One clear action at a time.
A visible result tells you what just happened.
Kūro crossed. A short path with visible feedback helps visitors know how to proceed.
ex.jumpMsg: Kūro stays put. The next step is unclear, and a settings detour doesn’t show how the tool works.

b1.handoff: Nadia knows what she has: a logo, nothing else. Now: who is she remaking it for?

b4.rule: Tell the designer the goal, what people should feel; the designer chooses the means.

b9.rule: A brand is a family: the small version is drawn, not shrunk.

b5.rule: To print large you need the vector file: it stays sharp at every size.
b5.handoff: She knows which files to ask for; a proposal arrives, “all included”.

plate.a1: A post-office arcade at dusk: a long wooden counter with sealed envelopes and string-tied parcels, a brass letter scale, empty pigeon lofts on the roof.
plate.a2: A counting room at night: a wooden desk with closed ledgers and an open notebook of blank lines, a small iron strongbox, a calendar of empty squares, a lit lantern and the towers through the window.

pay.name: Route
pay.lore: Selma is an illustrator in Bordj Bou Arréridj; in the evenings she teaches the Lantern’s printmaking class. A publisher abroad wants to pay her for her illustrations. She does not yet know which way the money will travel.
pay.rule: Before the price, the route: which way the money comes in, and what that passage costs.

f.0: The rate matters, but it comes later. First the route: how your bank or the service receives the money, and at what cost.
f.1: Yes. The route first, the price after.
f.2: The invoice matters for a transfer, not its colour. Look at the route: the delay, the fees, and what your bank accepts.

pay.handoff: The publisher is waiting for an answer: bank transfer, platform, marketplace or crypto?
pay.decision: The route first, the price second.

bank.name: Exchange
bank.lore: To receive the publisher’s money, two services show her “0 fees”. Selma distrusts a zero that round.
bank.rule: A “0 fees” is checked in three places: the exchange, the transfer, the card and the withdrawal.

f.0: Yes. A rate worse than the market is a fee that does not say its name.
f.1: The logo says nothing about the price. The cost hides in the exchange rate applied: compare it with the market rate on the same day.
f.2: The follower count says nothing about what you pay. Look at the rate applied: its gap with the market is the real price.

bank.handoff: The service chosen, what to charge per day is still open.
bank.decision: Compare the rate applied, not the poster.

rate.name: Rate
rate.lore: The publisher asks for a day rate. Selma starts from the calculator’s figures before putting in her own.
rate.rule: A rate is worked out: what you want to keep, plus your costs, divided by the days actually billed.

f.0: Not all 22: some days go to prospecting, quotes, admin and time off. Divide by the days billed.
f.1: Yes. Divide by the days billed, not the days worked.
f.2: You cannot bill more days than you work. Fewer are left: prospecting, quotes and time off take their share.

rate.handoff: The rate set, the publisher says he pays at 60 days.
rate.decision: Divide by the days billed, not the days worked.

treso.name: Cash
treso.lore: The publisher pays at 60 days. Selma checks how many months she can last if nothing comes in until then.
treso.rule: Cash in hand is the number of months you last if nothing comes in as planned.

f.0: He will pay, but in two months. Until then you have to last: the client’s delay becomes your cash need.
f.1: Yes. The client’s payment delay becomes your need for cash.
f.2: One more expense eats into your cash cushion. Before saying yes, keep enough to last at least those two months.

treso.handoff: The books in order, a message from “support” lands in her inbox.
treso.decision: The client’s delay becomes my cash need.

crypto.name: Keys
crypto.lore: A message signed “support” arrives, looking official. It mentions the wallet Selma opened to have a look.
crypto.rule: In crypto, what you own is the key: the recovery phrase is given to no one.

f.0: No genuine support ever asks for it. Whoever reads your recovery phrase takes everything: it is a scam.
f.1: Yes. No support asks for it. Ever.
f.2: Not whole, not in pieces: the phrase recreates your keys, and no support asks for it. Ever.

crypto.handoff: Selma keeps her phrase to herself, and her books in order.
crypto.decision: My recovery phrase goes to no one.

route.desc: Finding clients, pricing, living with time zones, protecting your files and preparing to leave: a free atlas for working from anywhere.

plate.r1: A rooftop café terrace at dusk: a small table with an open notebook of blank pages, a phone and a glass of tea, string lights, the sea and white houses below.
plate.r2: A railway station hall at night: two round clocks without numerals showing different times, a bench, a luggage trolley with a backpack, a wall socket with its cable, tall arched windows.
plate.r3: A guesthouse room at dawn: an arched window onto the sea, a closed booklet and a plant on the ledge, a calendar of empty squares on the wall, a packed backpack by the door.

route.toKit: The Nomad kit and the fixed-price services are at the Bookshop’s counter.

n1.lore: Selma leaves Bordj for a season and takes her work along. To pay for the road she needs three clients a month; she starts by writing to people.
n1.rule: Clients can be counted: the ones you want, divided by the share who reply, then by the share who sign.

f.0: Yes. One signature per 40 messages, so 120 messages for 3 clients. Or a better message, or a better offer: both rates can be worked on.
f.1: Cutting prices does not make more people reply. Count: one signature per 40 messages, so 120 messages for 3 clients, or a better rate.
f.2: Waiting does not fill the month. Clients answer messages: at this pace, 120 for 3 signatures, or a better message.

n1.handoff: A first client replies: he wants a price.
n1.decision: One signature per 40 messages: aim for 120, or write better.

n2.lore: The first client wants a figure that will not move. Selma counts her days before she answers.
n2.rule: A project price: the day rate, times the days estimated, plus a margin for the unforeseen.

f.0: If the price was fixed and the scope unchanged, the overrun is not the client’s: that is what the margin is for.
f.1: Yes, if the price was firm. It is the Studio’s rule: “if the work overruns, the difference is on us”. If the scope changes, that is a new quote.
f.2: Splitting the overrun goes back on a fixed price. With the same scope, the margin pays for the unforeseen.

n2.handoff: The price accepted, it still has to go in the quote.
n2.decision: The margin pays for the unforeseen; the fixed price does not move.

n3.lore: Before starting, Selma writes her quote: what is included, and what is not.
n3.rule: A signed quote answers the awkward questions in advance: the scope, the deposit, the revisions, the ownership, the deadline.

f.0: Not that one: at the Studio, two rounds per stage are included. The third is priced separately.
f.1: Yes. Two rounds per stage are included; further ones are quoted separately.
f.2: It is not refused: the Studio’s quote prices it separately, beyond the two rounds included per stage.

n3.handoff: The quote signed, the kick-off call has to fit a client six time zones further west.
n3.decision: Two rounds per stage, the rest priced apart: it is in the quote.

n4.lore: Selma is at UTC+1, her client at UTC−5. She looks for the hour where their two days meet.
n4.rule: Calls go in the hours the two days share; the rest is done in writing.

f.0: At 10:00 your time it is 4:00 for your client: his day has not begun. Look for the hours your two days share.
f.1: Yes. 16:00 for you is 10:00 for your client: the hour falls inside both days.
f.2: At 23:00 your time, your day is over. Put the call in the shared hours: 16:00 for you, 10:00 for him.

n4.handoff: The call set, Selma takes the train again, the laptop and the drive in the same bag.

n5.lore: On the night train her whole office fits in one bag: the laptop, the backup drive, the cables.
n5.rule: Three copies, on two devices, one of them kept outside the bag.

f.0: A password guards access, not the files that left with the bag. What was missing was a copy kept elsewhere.
f.1: Yes. That is the “1” in 3-2-1: one copy outside the bag, online or with someone you trust.
f.2: A second laptop in the same bag would go with the first. What was missing was a copy outside the bag.

n5.handoff: The copies safe, Selma has to log in at the airport.
n5.decision: Three copies, two devices, one elsewhere.

n6.lore: At the airport, Selma has to open her work email before boarding.
n6.rule: On the road your accounts are worth more than your kit: a network you control, two-step verification, one password per account.

f.0: ANSSI and the NCSC both advise avoiding networks you do not control. Go through your phone’s mobile network.
f.1: Yes. The mobile network rather than a network you do not control: that is the NCSC’s advice, and ANSSI’s.
f.2: A public computer is no more yours than public Wi-Fi. The safest is still your phone’s hotspot.

n6.handoff: Landed, Selma adds up her week.
n6.decision: The phone’s network rather than public Wi-Fi.

n7.lore: On the guesthouse terrace, Selma counts her days: five worked, but how many billed?
n7.rule: A year has 52 weeks, but you bill only part of them: count your billed days before promising yourself an income.

f.0: Not all five: prospecting, quotes, admin and learning take days too. At 60%, that makes 3 billed days.
f.1: Yes. The other two days are real: prospecting, quotes, paperwork, learning. Your day rate is what pays for them.
f.2: Fewer than five, but not that few: 60% of 5 days is 3 billed days.

n7.handoff: The season ends; before the next trip, the days of stay are still to be counted.
n7.decision: My rate also pays for the days not billed.

n8.lore: For the next season, Selma plans the Schengen area, with one day out in the middle.
n8.rule: Before the ticket, four files: the stay, taxes, health, the bank. The questions here, the answers from those who give them.

f.0: One day out erases nothing: you count 180 days back from each day of the stay.
f.1: Yes. You count back 180 days from each day of your stay: leaving for a day erases nothing. The Commission’s calculator does the count for you.
f.2: The counter does not pause: it looks at the 180 days before, on each day of the stay.

n8.handoff: The book is full: Selma heads home to Bordj.
n8.decision: Count over 180 days, with the Commission’s calculator.

act.j3: Act III · The price and the limit

plate.j1: A small arcade at night: two game cabinets with dark screens under a striped awning, a shelf of soft toys, a checkerboard floor, warm lantern light.
plate.j2: A corner of the Bookshop’s stall: a cork board of cream loyalty cards, a rubber stamp and an inkpad, a small trophy cup, a sheet of star stickers, under the striped awning.
plate.j3: A reading room at night: one armchair under a lamp, a closed handheld console on a shelf among books, an abstract framed print on the wall, a doorway open onto the towers.

g1.name: Level 1
g1.lore: The Lantern’s bookseller wants the night-class students to come back. Before talking loyalty cards, she looks up what gamification means.
g1.rule: Gamification lends a game’s spring to an activity that stays the real thing.

f.0: A whole game is a game, not gamification: gamification borrows a game’s spring for an activity that is not one.
f.1: Yes. The course is still a course; the bar lends it one of a game’s springs: seeing that you are moving forward.
f.2: A mascot alone is decoration. If you take the game away and nothing useful remains, it was not gamification.

g1.handoff: A loyalty card, then? Which need it would feed is still open.
g1.decision: The class stays a class; it borrows one spring from games.

g2.name: Level 2
g2.lore: The card would show the sessions already attended. The bookseller wonders what that is for.
g2.rule: A good game feeds three needs: feeling capable, free, connected.

f.0: Yes: it shows the road already covered. It is competence made visible.
f.1: Freedom is choosing your path and your pace. A progress bar mostly shows the way already done: that is competence.
f.2: Connection is playing with others. A progress bar shows what you have already done: it feeds the need to feel capable.

g2.handoff: The need found, the bookseller wants to know whether it really works.
g2.decision: The card shows the way done: it serves competence.

g3.name: Level 3
g3.lore: Before paying the printer, the bookseller reads what the studies say.
g3.rule: Real, modest effects that depend on context: nothing more to promise.

f.0: The studies find small but real effects, not all equally solid, and dependent on context. No serious person promises “every time”.
f.1: Yes: real, modest effects that depend on the context. Nobody serious promises more.
f.2: The studies do find effects, small but real, when gamification is designed for its audience.

g3.handoff: Cautious, she moves on to the mechanics, one by one.
g3.decision: Real, modest effects: promise nothing more.

g4.name: Level 4
g4.lore: The printer offers two card designs for the same number of sessions. The bookseller hesitates.
g4.rule: You pick one or two mechanics for a purpose, not ten for decoration.

f.0: The same effort, but nothing has started. The ten-box card with two already stamped is finished more often: that is endowed progress.
f.1: Yes. The same effort, but you have already started: that is the endowed progress effect.
f.2: Nunes and Drèze found a difference: the card that starts at 2 of 10 is finished more often, and faster.

g4.handoff: The card drawn, what it says about the Lantern remains.
g4.decision: A card that starts with two boxes stamped.

g5.name: Level 5
g5.lore: A card is also a voice. The bookseller wonders what hers will say about the Lantern.
g5.rule: Play gives a brand a voice, a world and a reason to come back; it serves the message, it does not replace it.

f.0: This level is a practitioners’ reading: what a brand gains first is a character people recognise, not data.
f.1: Yes. The rest may follow, but character is what brings people back.
f.2: Clicks may follow, but what brings people back is character: a voice, a world, a ritual.

g5.handoff: Before launching her card, the bookseller looks at real cases.
g5.decision: The Lantern keeps its voice: that is what brings people back.

g6.name: Level 6
g6.lore: Someone quotes impressive figures to the bookseller. She asks where they come from.
g6.rule: Read where a figure comes from: a published study, a company, or a brand campaign.

f.0: Starbucks’s figure comes from the company itself: useful, to be read as such. The scientific paper is Foldit.
f.1: Yes. The others are company or campaign figures: useful, and to be read as such.
f.2: The speed camera lottery is a famous but fragile case, from a campaign. The scientific paper is Foldit.

g6.handoff: The figures read, the bookseller looks for where it breaks.
g6.decision: Read where a figure comes from before believing it.

g7.name: Level 7
g7.lore: The bookseller was thinking of promising a discount at the end of the card. First she checks what makes such projects fail.
g7.rule: Play can demotivate, push, trap: most failures come from the design.

f.0: Gartner does not say people dislike playing: it forecast failures mostly because of poor design.
f.1: Yes. It is not the game that fails, it is the game badly thought out for its goal.
f.2: Gartner does not point at the technology; it points at poor design.

g7.handoff: The rules of her card are still to be written.
g7.decision: No pressure, no reward promised in advance.

g8.name: Level 8
g8.lore: The bookseller writes her card’s rules by looking at how this site plays.
g8.rule: Nothing starts by itself, the price does not play, a drawing rather than a discount, nothing leaves here, no pressure.

f.0: No discount here: seven seals open a drawing. No reward is traded for a purchase.
f.1: Yes. That is our rule: we reward with something to look at, never with pressure to buy.
f.2: There is no account and no ranking: the seals stay in your browser, and they open a drawing.

g8.decision: The Lantern’s card gives a print from the class, never a discount.

w1.rule: Signing means agreeing: you do not sign what you do not understand.

w8.rule: The hash says “sent”; only the receipt says whether it worked.

w8.foldNote: exercise folded: your route is the ordinary one, with no chain

w4.rule: A complete proposal also shows what is paid for after launch.
w4.handoff: The after-launch lines are noted; the supplier comes back by private message.
w4.decision: Ask for the after-launch lines, even without figures.

w5.rule: A completed transaction cannot be called back: urgency and a look-alike link are the signs.
w5.handoff: Samia did not click; the law is left, where her members are.
w5.decision: Do not click: a completed transaction does not come back.

w6.rule: The law that counts is the law where your users are: in Dubai, VARA.
w6.handoff: The law card is read; everything comes together on the brief.
w6.decision: For a token in Dubai: a VARA-licensed provider, or its consent.

w7.rule: The law first, the code second.
w7.handoff: Samia’s brief is ready to go, whenever she wants.
w7.decision: Have the law of the users’ countries checked before paying for development.
